questions.q: What does a commit's parent pointer refer to?
options: The branch it will eventually be merged into
The commit that came immediately before it
The staging area it was committed from
questions.explain: Each commit points back to its parent — the commit immediately before it — and that chain of pointers is what forms a repository's history.

questions.q: What command shows the full message, metadata, and diff for one specific commit?
questions.explain: git show <hash> displays everything about a single commit — message, author, date, and the full diff of what it changed.

questions.q: A commit's SHA-1 hash is calculated from:
options: Only the file names that changed
The commit's content, its parent, its author, and its message
The current system clock time only
questions.explain: The hash is derived from the commit's full content including its parent, author, and message — which is why it changes completely if anything about the commit is different, and why it reliably detects tampering.

questions.q: Which command would show what changed between two specific commits, 7c1e8d4 and a3f5c92?
questions.explain: git diff given two commit hashes (or branch names) shows everything that changed between those two points — with no arguments it instead compares the working directory to the last commit.

questions.q: Which commit message best follows the conventions this lesson recommends?
questions.explain: A good commit message is a short, specific, imperative summary of what changed and, ideally, why — not a vague placeholder like 'updates' or 'Fixed stuff.'
